analysis.one_liner: Ends tax breaks, royalty discounts, and federal financing for oil, gas, and coal companies.
analysis.headline: Introduced with six Democratic cosponsors in May 2024, the bill was sent to the Senate Finance Committee the same day and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would strip away the special tax treatment, reduced royalty payments, and federal financing that oil, gas, and coal companies receive. It would raise the royalties companies pay to drill or mine on public land from 12.5% to 18.75%, remove the cap on their liability for oil spills, increase the coal excise tax that funds black lung benefits for miners, and block US agencies and export-credit banks from financing fossil fuel projects. It would also repeal the law that fast-tracked the Mountain Valley Pipeline.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who currently subsidize production by highly profitable fossil fuel companies through dozens of tax breaks and below-market royalties on public land. People living near offshore drilling and pipelines gain from unlimited spill liability, and coal miners gain because a higher industry-paid excise tax funds the Black Lung Disability Trust Fund.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and communities near fossil fuel operations

how_it_helps.text: Terminates dozens of oil, gas, and coal tax breaks, including percentage depletion, immediate expensing of drilling costs, LIFO inventory accounting for oil and coal companies, capital gains treatment of coal royalties, and the corporate tax exemption for publicly traded fossil fuel partnerships.

Raises the royalty rate companies pay to extract oil, gas, and coal from federal land from 12.5% to 18.75%, and permanently bans royalty relief on offshore leases, so the public gets closer to full value for publicly owned resources.

Removes the liability cap for offshore oil facilities, makes pipelines carrying tar-sands oil fully liable for spills, denies tax deductions for spill damages, and ends the liability shield that banks with over $10 billion in assets enjoy under the Superfund law.

Increases the excise tax that funds the Black Lung Disability Trust Fund from $1.10 to $1.38 per ton (and from 55 to 69 cents for reduced-rate coal), shifting the cost of miners' benefits onto coal companies.

Prohibits the Export-Import Bank, the Development Finance Corporation, and other US agencies from financing fossil fuel projects, and rescinds US contributions to international financial institutions that fund them.

Repeals the Fiscal Responsibility Act provisions that mandated approval of the Mountain Valley Pipeline and shortened environmental reviews, restoring the public's ability to challenge major fossil fuel projects.

analysis.who_pays: Oil, gas, and coal companies, which would lose their tax preferences, pay higher royalties and excise taxes on public-land production, face a new 13% severance tax on Gulf of Mexico output, and become fully liable for spills and Superfund cleanup. Some of these costs could be passed on to consumers through fuel and electricity prices.

drawbacks.text: Eliminating drilling, mining, and refining tax preferences raises production costs, and producers can pass part of that through to households as higher prices for gasoline, heating fuel, and electricity.

The bill terminates the 45Q carbon capture credit and blocks Department of Energy loan funds for carbon capture and most hydrogen projects, removing subsidies some see as necessary tools for decarbonizing heavy industry.
Repealing the permitting and environmental-review changes in the Fiscal Responsibility Act would lengthen and complicate federal review of major infrastructure, not only fossil fuel projects.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The subsidies being repealed are direct transfers to some of the most profitable companies in the country, financed by general taxpayers, and the bill shifts cleanup and health costs (oil spills, black lung) back onto the industries that create them. The honest costs are possible consumer price pass-through, the loss of carbon capture subsidies that divide climate advocates, and slower federal permitting. On balance, the transfer being ended is much larger than the risks it carries, though the bill's breadth would have made for a difficult transition.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Bernie Sanders introduced the bill on May 23, 2024, joined by six Democratic cosponsors: Senators Merkley, Booker, Van Hollen, Welch, Warren, and Markey.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day.
No further action was ever taken: the bill received no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote, and no companion action before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil, gas, and coal companies, which kept every tax break, royalty discount, and liability cap the bill would have repealed, at no cost to themselves.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever held; the bill's seven sponsors were Senator Sanders and six of 48 Senate Democrats, and no Republican ever cosponsored it.

industries.note: The bill repeals their core tax preferences (intangible drilling cost expensing, percentage depletion, LIFO accounting, bonus depreciation for fossil fuel property), raises federal royalties to 18.75%, imposes a 13% Gulf of Mexico severance tax, and removes offshore spill liability caps. Their interest in keeping these benefits runs directly against taxpayers, who finance them.

The bill ends percentage depletion and capital gains treatment for coal royalties, raises Powder River Basin-area royalties, doubles down on the black lung excise so companies rather than taxpayers fund miners' benefits, and ends refined-coal credits.

It strips the Superfund (CERCLA) liability shield from banks with over $10 billion in assets and investment firms with over $250 billion under management when they lend to polluting sites, exposing them to cleanup costs.
It repeals the Fiscal Responsibility Act section that ordered approval of the Mountain Valley Pipeline and stripped courts of jurisdiction over its challenges.

The bill terminates the 45Q sequestration credit and limits DOE loan programs, but rewrites the clean hydrogen credit to require truly renewable electricity — hurting fossil-linked capture projects while steering remaining support toward cleaner production.
